text: You are building a developer productivity agent (Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude) that integrates two MCP tools: `analyze_content` ("Analyzes content and returns insights") and `analyze_document` ("Analyzes documents and returns insights"). Logs show the agent frequently calls `analyze_content` when a user pastes a URL to a web article, and calls `analyze_document` when asked to review a PDF uploaded earlier in the session—but roughly 30% of the time the tools are swapped, producing failed or irrelevant results. Both tools accept a generic `source` string parameter. What is the most effective fix?
options: Lower the temperature parameter on API calls so the model makes more deterministic tool selections

Rename the tools and rewrite their descriptions to be purpose-specific (e.g., `extract_web_results` for live URLs, `extract_pdf_content` for uploaded documents), each specifying accepted input formats and example use cases
Merge both tools into a single `analyze_source` tool and let the model infer the content type from the input string at runtime
Add a retry loop that re-prompts the model whenever a tool call fails, asking it to try the other tool instead
correct_answer: Rename the tools and rewrite their descriptions to be purpose-specific (e.g., `extract_web_results` for live URLs, `extract_pdf_content` for uploaded documents), each specifying accepted input formats and example use cases
explanation: Tool descriptions are the primary signal an LLM uses for tool selection. Near-identical descriptions on functionally overlapping tools (like `analyze_content` vs `analyze_document`) cause exactly this kind of misrouting. The fix is to differentiate the tools by name and description—clarifying input formats, example queries, and boundaries—so the model can reliably distinguish them (B). Lowering temperature (A) doesn't address ambiguous tool semantics. Merging the tools (C) reintroduces ambiguity rather than resolving it, since the model still has to infer intent from a generic parameter. Retrying after failure (D) treats the symptom, wasting calls and latency instead of fixing the root cause of unreliable selection.

text: In your customer support resolution agent (Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent), the `process_refund` MCP tool currently returns a generic string `"Operation failed"` whenever it cannot complete a refund, whether due to a backend timeout, an invalid order ID, or a policy violation (refund amount exceeds the allowed threshold). Agents using this tool either retry indefinitely on policy violations or give up immediately on recoverable timeouts. What change to the tool's error response would best resolve this?
options: Have the tool always return `isError: false` and embed the failure explanation as plain text in the result, so the model doesn't halt the agentic loop
Increase the tool's internal retry count so that transient and business errors are both retried automatically before returning to the agent
Replace the error string with an HTTP status code only, relying on the model's general knowledge of status code meanings to decide how to proceed
Return structured error metadata including an `errorCategory` (transient/validation/permission/business), an `isRetryable` boolean, and a human-readable description specific to the failure
correct_answer: Return structured error metadata including an `errorCategory` (transient/validation/permission/business), an `isRetryable` boolean, and a human-readable description specific to the failure
explanation: Uniform, generic error responses prevent the agent from making appropriate recovery decisions. Returning structured error metadata (D) lets the agent distinguish transient failures (worth retrying) from business-rule violations like exceeding a refund threshold (not retryable, requiring a different workflow such as escalation) and from validation or permission errors. Always returning `isError: false` (A) would hide genuine failures from the agent, undermining the MCP error-signaling pattern. Auto-retrying business errors (B) is incorrect since retries can't fix a policy violation. A bare HTTP status code (C) lacks the business-specific context (e.g., refund threshold exceeded) needed for the agent to respond appropriately to the customer.

text: In your multi-agent research system (Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System), the coordinator currently grants all four subagents (web search, document analysis, synthesis, report generation) access to the full set of 18 available tools, reasoning that this maximizes flexibility. You observe the synthesis subagent occasionally attempting raw web searches instead of requesting that data from the web search subagent, and overall tool selection accuracy has degraded across all subagents. What is the best architectural change?
options: Scope each subagent's tool access to only what its role requires (e.g., synthesis gets a lightweight `verify_fact` tool but not full web search), routing complex cross-role needs through the coordinator
Keep all 18 tools available to every subagent but add a system prompt note instructing each subagent to 'only use tools relevant to your role'
Set `tool_choice: "any"` for every subagent so the model is forced to call some tool on every turn, preventing idle subagents
Consolidate all 18 tools into a single mega-tool with a `task_type` parameter so subagents only interact with one tool interface
correct_answer: Scope each subagent's tool access to only what its role requires (e.g., synthesis gets a lightweight `verify_fact` tool but not full web search), routing complex cross-role needs through the coordinator
explanation: Giving an agent access to many more tools than its role requires increases decision complexity and degrades tool selection reliability, and agents equipped with out-of-specialization tools (like a synthesis agent with web search) tend to misuse them. The correct fix is restricting each subagent's tools to its role (A), while providing a narrow, high-frequency cross-role tool (like `verify_fact`) where justified, and routing more complex cross-role needs through the coordinator. A prompt-based instruction to 'only use relevant tools' (B) is a probabilistic guideline, not a structural fix, and doesn't reduce the actual decision space. Forcing `tool_choice: "any"` (C) doesn't address which tools are available, only whether a tool must be called. Merging everything into one mega-tool (D) reintroduces ambiguity and doesn't solve the underlying over-provisioning problem.

text: Your team is setting up MCP integrations for Claude Code across the engineering organization (Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude). You need a shared GitHub MCP server that every developer on the team uses with a common configuration, authenticated via a personal access token that must never be committed to version control. One engineer also wants to experiment with a personal, unreleased MCP server for a side project, without affecting teammates. How should these be configured?
options: Configure both servers in the project-level `.mcp.json`, hardcoding the GitHub token directly since `.mcp.json` is excluded from version control by default
Configure the shared GitHub server in `~/.claude.json` so each developer can customize the token individually, and put the experimental server in `.mcp.json` since it's not yet team-wide

Configure the shared GitHub server in the project-level `.mcp.json` using `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` environment variable expansion for the credential, and have the engineer configure their experimental server in their user-level `~/.claude.json`
Configure both servers in a single `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` file using inline `@import` statements to reference each server's connection details
correct_answer: Configure the shared GitHub server in the project-level `.mcp.json` using `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` environment variable expansion for the credential, and have the engineer configure their experimental server in their user-level `~/.claude.json`
explanation: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` is the correct place for shared, team-wide MCP tooling, and it is checked into version control—so environment variable expansion (`${GITHUB_TOKEN}`) is essential to avoid committing secrets directly. Personal or experimental servers that shouldn't affect teammates belong in the user-scoped `~/.claude.json` (option C). Option A incorrectly assumes `.mcp.json` is excluded from version control and risks leaking a credential. Option B reverses the intended scoping, making the shared server a per-developer configuration and the personal experiment team-wide. `CLAUDE.md` files (option D) are for instructions/context, not MCP server connection configuration.

text: While exploring an unfamiliar legacy codebase (Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude), your agent is tasked with finding every place in the codebase that imports and calls a utility function named `formatCurrency`, then updating each call site to pass a new `locale` parameter. The function is re-exported under different aliases from several barrel files. What is the most reliable tool-usage sequence for this task?
options: Use `Glob` to locate every `.js` file in the repository, then `Read` each file fully to manually scan for calls to `formatCurrency`

Use `Grep` to find all exported aliases of `formatCurrency` across barrel files, then use `Grep` again to search for each alias name across the codebase, then use `Edit` (falling back to `Read`+`Write` when anchor text isn't unique) to update each call site
Use `Bash` with a single shell pipeline combining `find` and `sed` to rewrite all call sites in one pass without first identifying aliases
Use `Write` to overwrite each file suspected of containing a call site, regenerating the entire file content from scratch based on the agent's understanding of the codebase
correct_answer: Use `Grep` to find all exported aliases of `formatCurrency` across barrel files, then use `Grep` again to search for each alias name across the codebase, then use `Edit` (falling back to `Read`+`Write` when anchor text isn't unique) to update each call site
explanation: `Grep` is the right tool for content search—finding exported aliases and then locating each alias's usages across the codebase—which correctly handles the re-export/aliasing complexity. `Edit` is appropriate for targeted modifications using unique anchor text, with `Read`+`Write` as the documented fallback when `Edit` cannot find a unique match (option B). Using `Glob` plus reading every file (A) wastes context and doesn't handle aliasing logic. A blind `Bash` `find`+`sed` pipeline (C) skips identifying aliases first and risks incorrect or incomplete rewrites with no verification. Using `Write` to regenerate whole files (D) risks destructive, inaccurate changes compared to targeted `Edit` operations.
